content.text:
Three separate mechanisms start background brain processes. On this machine the launchd watcher is running now (PID 55830, label `io.entire.brain-watch.a2d3fd66`), and one `memory worker --once` was running when I checked (PID 71524).

### 1. The launchd/systemd watcher (always running)
- **What it runs:** `entire-brain workspace watch --distill`. There is one per machine, and it restarts forever (`KeepAlive`).
- **Who installs it:** `entire brain setup`, via `resolveSetupSteps` in [setup.go:1282](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup.go:1282). That calls `brainWatchDaemonPlan` ([setup.go:1119](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup.go:1119)) and then `launchctl load -w` ([setup_daemon.go:557](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_daemon.go:557)).
- **Controls:** these setup flags at [setup.go:471](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup.go:471):
  - `--no-daemon` and `--uninstall-daemon`
  - `--interval` (poll interval) and `--distill-every` (minimum gap between agent runs)
  - The env var `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DAEMON_NO_REGISTER` writes the unit file but never calls launchctl.

### 2. The one-shot fact backfill (setup only)
- `spawnDetached` in [setup_spawn.go:23](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:23) starts it with `Setsid` and releases the handle. `setup` is the only non-test caller.
- **Controls:** `--no-backfill`, `--agent`, `--model`, `--backfill-budget`.

### 3. `memory worker --once` (starts on events, from four places)
All four go through `memoryWorkerLaunchAfter` in [memory_cmd.go:111](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:111). It runs `exec.Command(os.Executable(), "memory","worker","--once")` and reaps the child in a goroutine.
- **Agent hooks:** `memory notify` and `hook session-end` call `recordMemoryLifecycleAndLaunch` ([memory_cmd.go:196](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:196)).
- **Each watch tick:** [watch.go:420](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/watch.go:420) and [watch.go:646](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/watch.go:646) call `reconcileMemoryAndLaunch`. This means #1 keeps starting #3.
- **MCP server startup:** `nudgeMemoryAtStartup` ([memory_cmd.go:234](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:234)) is called from [mcp.go:130](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/mcp.go:130).
- **The worker itself:** it relaunches itself with a delay or backoff ([memory_cmd.go:1658](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:1658)).

What limits it:
- A coordinator lock (`memory-worker.lock`). A second worker exits with `AlreadyActive`.
- `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MEMORY_WORKER=1` ([memory_coordinator.go:20](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_coordinator.go:20)) only stops the MCP startup path from nudging a worker when it is already running inside one.

There is no user-facing switch that turns the memory worker off.

**Tooling limits:**
- Graph doesn't index function values stored in package variables (`memoryWorkerLaunch*`), so I found those call sites with `rg`.
- Brain's index is from `main@cc15181`, not this branch, and its brief had no recorded reasoning for this design. Everything above was checked against current source.

**Next:** run `launchctl list | rg entire` before and after a Claude session ends to see the hook-triggered workers appear.

content.content:
entire-brain is an external-command plugin for the Entire CLI.

It builds a local, inspectable repository brain from retained sessions, seed
context, docs, history, semantic records, and durable facts, then exposes
retrieval, verification, evaluation, and MCP surfaces for agents.

Usage:
  entire-brain [flags]
  entire-brain [command]

Set up the brain & agents:
  setup          Build the brain and start background updates
  add            Clone a repository, fetch its Entire history, and build its brain
  init-agents    Install coordinated agent instructions
  agent-guide    Preview repository-specific agent instructions
  mcp            Serve local brain tools over MCP (stdio by default, or HTTP with --http)
  webhook        Notify another service when this brain changes
  config         Inspect or initialize plugin configuration

Search & explore the brain:
  overview       Summarize the project, its structure, and decisions
  brief          Gather relevant context for a task
  query          Search the brain (hybrid by default)
  get            Fetch a brain item by ID
  multi-get      Fetch multiple brain items by ID
  dash           Browse the brain in an interactive dashboard

Durable facts & patterns:
  recall         Retrieve durable facts matching a query for the current branch
  remember       Record a durable fact about this repository
  distill        Extract durable facts from sessions (requires an agent)
  facts          Review, promote, and garbage-collect durable facts
  verify         Verify durable fact anchors against local retained sources
  patterns       Inspect and rebuild recurring patterns from sessions

Sessions & conversation memory:
  memory         Manage conversation indexing and background jobs
  privacy        Control which captured sessions the brain retains

Code & semantic index:
  inspect        Explore code, dependencies, and change history
  show           Show one semantic brain record
  entities       Find checkpoints and sessions that changed a symbol
  viz            Explore the brain as a graph in your browser
  repair         Rebuild derived semantic indexes

Brain state & maintenance:
  status         Show brain coverage, freshness, and workspace state
  stats          Show brain record counts and breakdowns
  docs           Inspect how non-code documents are read into the brain
  refresh        Create or refresh the repository brain
  watch          Keep the brain up to date automatically
  gc             Prune old local semantic overlays and snapshots
  reset          Remove local generated brain data

Workspaces & sharing:
  workspace      Manage local multi-repo brain workspaces
  bundle         Import or export local brain bundles
  publish        Publish the local brain to hosted Entire (opt-in)

----
Available Commands:
  abstract    Inspect or explicitly generate an optional evidence-linked session abstract
  cancel      Cancel work cooperatively; repeats are idempotent unless completion already won
  configure   Manage optional memory feature selection
  jobs        List content-free work metadata
  migrate     Upgrade derived schemas atomically (build beside, switch, never delete first)
  notify      Record a content-free host lifecycle hint (session_start | checkpoint | session_end) and nudge the worker
  rebuild     Recreate the disposable projections from the canonical captured sessions
  reconcile   Compare canonical sessions with projection receipts and enqueue missing work
  repair      Verify projection dependencies and perform the smallest deterministic rebuild
  retry       Move failed or invalid work to pending; repeated pending retries are idempotent
  status      Report hint, job, and projection-receipt health

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for memory

Use "entire-brain memory [command] --help" for more information about a command.
----
Available Commands:
  add         Add a local repository to a workspace by repo key
  create      Create a local workspace brain
  get         Fetch items in full by repo-qualified id (e.g. gh/owner/repo/fact:… or gh/owner/repo/conversation:…, as printed by workspace search)
  inspect     Run specialist inspection commands across workspace repos
  list        List local workspaces
  patterns    Inspect and rebuild cross-repo patterns for a workspace
  query       Hybrid (lexical+vector, RRF) search across every workspace repo's brain
  refresh     Refresh local workspace membership freshness (--full also refreshes each member brain)
  remove      Remove a repo from a workspace, or delete the whole workspace
  review      Diff-less review across workspace repos: suspected regressions as severity-ranked findings
  watch       Keep every repo in a workspace fresh automatically (deterministic refresh is free; agent steps gated)

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for workspace

Use "entire-brain workspace [command] --help" for more information about a command.

content.text:
There's no single stop command. The closest per process:

| Process | How to stop it | What happens next |
|---|---|---|
| Watcher (`workspace watch --distill`) | `entire brain setup --uninstall-daemon` | Removed for good. There's no pause; you get it back by running `setup` again. |
| Fact backfill | `kill` its PID by hand. `stopDetachedProcess` exists, but setup only calls it ([setup.go:996](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup.go:996)) when it fails to write the backfill state file. | Stops. |
| `memory worker --once` | `entire brain memory cancel <job-id>` cancels a job cooperatively, not the worker. | The next agent hook, watch tick or MCP start launches a new worker. |

So to make the brain go quiet right now (fish):

```fish
entire brain setup --uninstall-daemon
kill (entire brain status --json | jq '.onboarding.facts.pid // empty')
pkill -f 'entire-brain memory worker'
```

Even then, the next session-end hook or MCP server start launches a new memory worker. Nothing in the code checks a "paused" flag before launching.

This branch is named `alex/control-background-processes`, so I assume this is the gap you're about to fill. The simplest version: one durable "paused" marker that all three launch points check first (`memoryWorkerLaunchAfter`, `spawnDetached`, and the watch tick), plus `brain stop`/`brain start` commands that set it and kill whatever is running. That's roughly an afternoon including tests.

Next: say whether you want the pause to apply to the whole machine or to one repo. That decides where the marker lives, and I can start once I know.

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

content.text:
`entire brain stop` and `entire brain start` now exist. `stop` pauses all background brain work on this machine; `start` resumes it. The 6 new tests pass and the built binary works. Nothing is committed yet.

**What `stop` does:**
- **Watcher:** stays loaded, because launchd would just restart it if it exited. Each tick it logs `[watch] paused — entire-brain start resumes` and does nothing else.
- **Memory workers:** hooks, watch ticks, MCP startup and the workers' own relaunches all still start a worker, but it exits at once and reports `"paused": true`. The check runs after the worker's sleep, so a worker that was already sleeping also stops. Work recorded while paused is kept and runs after `start`.
- **Setup backfill:** a new `setup` skips it and says why. If this repo's backfill is already running, `stop` kills it, using the same check `setup` relies on (the recorded PID is alive and the distill lock is held). A stale record is left alone, so an unrelated process that reused the PID is never killed.

The pause is a `paused` file in the plugin state directory, next to `watch-plan.json`. If that directory can't be read, the code treats it as not paused, so the brain doesn't silently stop updating.

**Verification:**
- `go test ./...`: one failure, `TestOllamaDistillAgentEnvelopeAllowanceIsCeilinged`. It fails the same way on the unmodified base commit, which I checked in a temporary worktree, so it was already broken.
- I ran `stop` → `start` on the built binary against temporary state directories, so your real watcher was never paused. Both commands appear under "Brain state & maintenance" in `--help`.

**Limits:**
- `stop` only kills the backfill of the repo you run it in. Backfills in other repos keep running, though `setup` starts them one at a time.
- A memory worker that is mid-pass finishes that bounded pass (at most 8 jobs).
- `brain status` doesn't show "paused" yet.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/alex/.claude/skills/pr-followup

# Pre-push verification — REQUIRED

Before `git push`, `gh pr create`, or any action that sends code to a remote, run the project's full pre-push verification on the current tree:

- **Go projects:** `gofmt -l .` (expect empty output) AND `golangci-lint run ./...` AND `go test ./...`. If the repo provides a wrapper like `mise run check` or `mise run lint`, prefer that — it's what CI runs.
- **Other ecosystems:** run the equivalent fmt + lint + test trio. Check `Makefile`, `package.json`, `mise.toml`, `justfile`, or similar for the canonical command.

Why all three, every time:

- CI runs gofmt and the linter as separate jobs that can fail independently. A clean `go test` with a dirty `gofmt -l` will fail CI and bounce the PR.
- gofmt failures are most common in test files — column-aligned struct literals get re-flowed by gofmt — so "test-only change" is not a reason to skip.
- If formatting changes anything, re-run the linter on the formatted tree; a prior clean lint result doesn't carry across a `gofmt -w`.
- This applies in every repo, not just the CLI. Smaller repos (libraries, internal tools) often lack a `mise` wrapper — run the underlying tools directly.

# Just prior to launching a PR — REQUIRED

Once development is 'finished':

- Size the diff: `git diff --numstat origin/main...HEAD`, ignoring generated files. Over 800 net changed lines, don't open the PR — split it, or state in the body why it's genuinely atomic. See `# PR sizing` in CLAUDE.md.

  Cut lines that work, in preference order:
  - **Mechanism before wiring** — the helper, type or script lands unused; the caller lands next.
  - **Delete before add** — remove the old path in its own PR before the replacement goes in.
  - **Infra before code** — overlay/config entries first, then the image, then the wiring.

- Check the branch is up to date with origin/main; update if not.
- Dispatch `slop-reviewer` and /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr together, in parallel, without asking for approval. Both are inputs to the same judgment, so there's no reason to serialise them. `slop-reviewer` mirrors Entire's trail-slop runner, so its rating predicts what the trail will say before you push.
- When both land, the slop rating sets what you do with the findings: `small` → address the toolkit's findings and proceed; `medium` → fix slop's cited findings too, then re-run it; `large` → **don't open the PR**. A `large` is friction, not a backlog — the core approach needs reshaping, and the toolkit's findings feed that reshape rather than a patch pass.

# After launching a PR

**Who owns the loop?** Per CLAUDE.md the default is a `review-steward` agent — one per PR, the single writer in that PR's checkout. If one is (or will be) dispatched, stop here: your role becomes forwarding wake signals and handling its escalations, and you consume its summary instead of polling. Work the sections below yourself only when no steward is dispatched — a trivial, single PR.

## The three feedback channels

They conclude on independent clocks. Poll each and act the moment any ONE has work; never wait for "all checks terminal" before starting.

- **Bugbot / GitHub review threads.** Poll the "Cursor Bugbot" check_run on the current head for a non-null conclusion — {success, neutral, failure/skipping} all mean it has finished posting. The conclusion's *value* proves nothing: `success` does NOT guarantee no comments, since they post asynchronously and can land with or after the conclusion. Once it is terminal, fetch unresolved threads directly via the `github-pr-review` skill (`pr-threads`); that fetch is authoritative. Never grep `gh pr checks` for pass/fail keywords. A red X is blocking, not advisory. Re-fetch after any rebase or force-push — comment IDs change.

  **Causing a signal and waiting for one are two separate steps.** A push does NOT retrigger bugbot at all — the `bugbot run` top-level comment does; verified empirically, no check_run exists on the new head until it lands, even though CI re-runs on its own. So comment first, then confirm a check_run actually **exists** on the current head before waiting on it. Waiting for "terminal on the current head" when bugbot has no check_run there at all burns the entire timeout on a signal that was never coming. Any watcher's precondition must itself be checked: does the thing I am waiting for even exist yet?
- **Trail findings.** CLI-only and **invisible on GitHub** — a green gate or "Findings: passed" does not mean none exist. `entire trail finding list --freshness any`, run from the PR's worktree, is authoritative — `--freshness` defaults to `current`, so the bare command hides stale-but-open findings that still block the gate. Use full finding ids, never a truncated suffix. The trail review runs on its own cadence, so findings can appear before, after, or without bugbot. Findings regenerate on a **tree change**, not a new commit sha: a trailer-only amend leaves the tree byte-identical and won't resurrect an adjudicated finding, so metadata amends are safe to push late in an endgame.
- **CI.** Any check_run at `failure` → read its output and fix now. Another check sitting `in_progress` never blocks that.

**Never act on the `Entire Gates` rollup conclusion.** It aggregates three sub-gates — Approvals, Checks, Findings — and the breakdown is in its `output.summary`. A `failure` whose only failing sub-gate is **Approvals** is merge-ready (approvals are out of scope, below). Only Checks or Findings are actionable, and cross-check Findings against `entire trail finding list --freshness any` — the CLI wins when they disagree.

## Arming the Monitor

Detection must not be able to die. Use `Monitor` with `persistent: true` — a self-re-arming agent or a bounded bash poll both hit a ceiling and go quiet, and silence reads as "still running."

- Emit ONLY on actionable transitions, tracking previous state so the same condition isn't re-emitted every poll; a firehose gets auto-stopped. Stay silent while work is progressing.
- Coverage must include the bad paths, not just the clean one: steady-state-reached, CI failure, steward stalled with work remaining, and N consecutive fetch failures → DEGRADED. A happy-path-only filter converts failure into silence.
- Give every watcher a timeout branch and a non-zero exit, and confirm it emitted at least once rather than assuming it is alive.
- These scripts run under **zsh** and **bash 3.2**. No `declare -A` — accumulate strings instead. Never put `[` directly after an expansion: `"#$pr[bb=$x]"` dies in zsh, where `$pr[...]` is an array subscript. Write `"#$pr bb=$x"`. Quote every expansion.

## The loop

1. Fix CI failures and accepted findings. Batch each wave into ONE commit and push, never one per finding. Write the failing test first where the bug is testable.
2. Verify before pushing — the full fmt + lint + test trio above.
3. **Resolve** every thread and finding you addressed. A reply, or a dismissal that leaves the GitHub thread unresolved (or the trail finding open), still counts as outstanding and still blocks the gate. GitHub threads resolve via GraphQL `resolveReviewThread` (`pr-reply` replies but does not resolve); trail findings via the `entire:address-findings` skill, which auto-applies suggested patches — or the CLI directly for dismissals, which that skill can't do.
4. If you pushed code, comment `bugbot run` as a top-level PR comment — required, not optional, since the push alone won't retrigger it — then confirm the new check_run exists on the new head before arming any wait. After a restructure, also resolve now-stale threads with a note on *why* they are structurally closed; bugbot re-lists unresolved findings on retrigger, so stale-but-open threads pollute the next wave.
5. Re-detect and repeat.

## Done

**0 unresolved review threads AND 0 open trail findings, by direct fetch** — and *stable*, not a one-shot read:

- A zero-count read only counts once bugbot is terminal on the **current** head SHA. Taken while it is queued/pending, the read is meaningless.
- The trail review settles independently and often later; it must have posted for the current code version too. One channel clearing says nothing about the other.
- **Human approval is out of scope** — never a blocker, never a wait condition. When the automated signals are clear, say merge-ready.

Then check whether the branch is behind, and give the user the Trail and PR URLs so they can click through.

content.text:
# Comprehensive PR Review

Run a comprehensive pull request review using multiple specialized agents, each focusing on a different aspect of code quality.

**Review Aspects (optional):** ""

## Review Workflow:

1. **Determine Review Scope**
   - Check git status to identify changed files
   - Parse arguments to see if user requested specific review aspects
   - Default: Run all applicable reviews

2. **Available Review Aspects:**

   - **comments** - Analyze code comment accuracy and maintainability
   - **tests** - Review test coverage quality and completeness
   - **errors** - Check error handling for silent failures
   - **types** - Analyze type design and invariants (if new types added)
   - **code** - General code review for project guidelines
   - **simplify** - Simplify code for clarity and maintainability
   - **all** - Run all applicable reviews (default)

3. **Identify Changed Files**
   - Run `git diff --name-only` to see modified files
   - Check if PR already exists: `gh pr view`
   - Identify file types and what reviews apply

4. **Determine Applicable Reviews**

   Based on changes:
   - **Always applicable**: code-reviewer (general quality)
   - **If test files changed**: pr-test-analyzer
   - **If comments/docs added**: comment-analyzer
   - **If error handling changed**: silent-failure-hunter
   - **If types added/modified**: type-design-analyzer
   - **After passing review**: code-simplifier (polish and refine)

5. **Launch Review Agents**

   **Sequential approach** (one at a time):
   - Easier to understand and act on
   - Each report is complete before next
   - Good for interactive review

   **Parallel approach** (user can request):
   - Launch all agents simultaneously
   - Faster for comprehensive review
   - Results come back together

6. **Aggregate Results**

   After agents complete, summarize:
   - **Critical Issues** (must fix before merge)
   - **Important Issues** (should fix)
   - **Suggestions** (nice to have)
   - **Positive Observations** (what's good)

7. **Provide Action Plan**

   Organize findings:
   ```markdown
   # PR Review Summary

   ## Critical Issues (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Issue description [file:line]

   ## Important Issues (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Issue description [file:line]

   ## Suggestions (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Suggestion [file:line]

   ## Strengths
   - What's well-done in this PR

   ## Recommended Action
   1. Fix critical issues first
   2. Address important issues
   3. Consider suggestions
   4. Re-run review after fixes
   ```

## Usage Examples:

**Full review (default):**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr
```

**Specific aspects:**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr tests errors
# Reviews only test coverage and error handling

/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr comments
# Reviews only code comments

/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr simplify
# Simplifies code after passing review
```

**Parallel review:**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr all parallel
# Launches all agents in parallel
```

## Agent Descriptions:

**comment-analyzer**:
- Verifies comment accuracy vs code
- Identifies comment rot
- Checks documentation completeness

**pr-test-analyzer**:
- Reviews behavioral test coverage
- Identifies critical gaps
- Evaluates test quality

**silent-failure-hunter**:
- Finds silent failures
- Reviews catch blocks
- Checks error logging

**type-design-analyzer**:
- Analyzes type encapsulation
- Reviews invariant expression
- Rates type design quality

**code-reviewer**:
- Checks CLAUDE.md compliance
- Detects bugs and issues
- Reviews general code quality

**code-simplifier**:
- Simplifies complex code
- Improves clarity and readability
- Applies project standards
- Preserves functionality

## Tips:

- **Run early**: Before creating PR, not after
- **Focus on changes**: Agents analyze git diff by default
- **Address critical first**: Fix high-priority issues before lower priority
- **Re-run after fixes**: Verify issues are resolved
- **Use specific reviews**: Target specific aspects when you know the concern

## Workflow Integration:

**Before committing:**
```
1. Write code
2. Run: /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr code errors
3. Fix any critical issues
4. Commit
```

**Before creating PR:**
```
1. Stage all changes
2. Run: /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr all
3. Address all critical and important issues
4. Run specific reviews again to verify
5. Create PR
```

**After PR feedback:**
```
1. Make requested changes
2. Run targeted reviews based on feedback
3. Verify issues are resolved
4. Push updates
```

## Notes:

- Agents run autonomously and return detailed reports
- Each agent focuses on its specialty for deep analysis
- Results are actionable with specific file:line references
- Agents use appropriate models for their complexity
- All agents available in `/agents` list

message.content: hmm, is it basically a cronjob, which is why this is so hard to stop?

content.text:
No, it isn't cron. It's harder to stop than cron, because there are three launchers instead of one schedule:

1. **The watcher is a launchd `KeepAlive` service, not a scheduled job.** It's one long-running `workspace watch --distill` process that loops and sleeps. If you kill it, launchd restarts it immediately ([setup_daemon.go:259](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_daemon.go:259)). To stop a cron job you delete one line; here, killing the process does nothing useful.
2. **Memory workers are started by events, not by a schedule.** Agent session-end hooks, MCP server startup and every watcher tick each launch a `memory worker --once`. So even with the watcher gone, finishing a Claude session starts one.
3. **Workers schedule their own next run.** A worker can relaunch itself with a delay of up to 2h for retries or follow-up work ([memory_cmd.go:1658](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:1658)). That leaves detached processes sleeping that nothing else tracks.

Each of these was designed to be robust on its own: never die, never miss an event, always retry. Nobody designed a shared off switch. That's why the change checks one marker inside all three paths instead of trying to kill processes: killing loses to `KeepAlive` and to the next hook.

The six reviewers are still running; I'll report their findings when they land.

     - No test covers the hook path.
     - Scores on: Severity (the feature's core promise is broken on the path that spends the most tokens per session) and Avoidability (the hook is next to the worker launch it calls).
  
  2. [internal/cli/pause.go:89](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:89) (`newStopCommand`): the resume hint hardcodes `` `entire brain start` ``.

     - The same diff uses that helper in `setup.go` but not here. Standalone users get a command their shell may not resolve.
     - Scores on: Avoidability.
  
  3. [internal/cli/pause.go:26-36](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:26) and the status surfaces: the pause is invisible outside the watch log, the worker JSON and setup.
     - `brain status` / `buildBrainOnboardingStatus` never reports it.
     - `backgroundPaused`'s own comment warns that "a brain that silently stops updating is worse". Yet a user who forgets they ran `stop` sees a healthy-looking status while nothing updates.
     - Scores on: Severity (low-moderate) and Avoidability.
  
  4. [internal/cli/pause.go:56-76](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:56) (`stopRepoBackfill`): only the current repo's backfill is killed, and errors resolving the repo or storage are silently swallowed (returns 0, nil).
     - Backfills started by `setup` in other repos keep spending tokens despite "machine-wide".
     - This is documented in the comment, so it is minor, but it adds to the gap between the headline and what the command does.
     - Scores on: Severity (low).

The tests do exercise the behaviour of the three gated paths, not just the marker text.

  ## Silent-failure review of `entire brain stop` / `start` (origin/main...HEAD, commit 4a641e1f)
  
  **Verdict:** Failing open in `backgroundPaused` is acceptable, but every failure it discards should be logged. The `(0, nil)` returns in `stopRepoBackfill` are not acceptable. In those cases `stop` prints "background brain work paused" while a backfill that spends tokens keeps running, and nothing tells the user. There is also a worse problem: one success path can SIGKILL a process that has nothing to do with brain.
  
  Tooling: Brain v0.1.0-nightly.202609300630 and Graph v0.4.1-nightly are available. The Brain index is stale (it was built from main 127df3ce, not this branch's HEAD), so every finding below was checked against current source. I did not run the tests. I found the helpers with `rg` as location lookups and did not run Graph neighbors/impact queries.
  
  ### 1. CRITICAL: `stop` can SIGKILL an unrelated process and report it as a backfill
  - [pause.go:68-75](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:68) calls `backfillRunning` and then `stopDetachedProcess` (`proc.Kill`).
  - `backfillRunning` leans towards "running" in two places:
    - [setup_spawn.go:125](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:125): if the lock is held by anyone, including the watch daemon's own distill pass, it returns true.
    - [setup_spawn.go:129](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:129): if the lock can't be read, it returns true.
  - That lean was chosen so setup avoids spawning a second backfill, which does no harm. Here it decides whether to kill.
  - `backfill.json` is written at [setup.go:998](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup.go:998) and is never cleared, so every repo that has run setup keeps an old pid on record indefinitely.
  - How it happens: the old pid gets reused by, say, the user's editor. The user runs `stop` while the daemon is partway through a pass (which is likely, since they are stopping work they can see running). The editor is SIGKILLed and the output says "stopped this repository's fact backfill (pid N)".
  - [pause_test.go:61](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause_test.go:61) only tests the case where the lock is free.
  - **Fix options:**
    - Don't kill anything (see the shared fix below).
    - Or check that the process holding the lock is the recorded pid. `writeLockOwnerMetadata` already records the owner, so compare that against `state.PID`.
    - In any case, don't reuse `backfillRunning` to decide on a kill.
  
  ### 2. HIGH: what `stop` actually stops depends on the current directory, and it says nothing when it skips
  - At [pause.go:60-67](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:60) these cases all return `(0, nil)` with no message:
    - `resolveLocalTargetRepoDir` fails (a stat error other than ENOENT, or an Abs error).
    - The target is not local.
    - `repoStoragePaths` fails. That includes `localRepoIdentityConflictError`, where the repo and its backfill are real.
  - A backfill in any other repo is never touched, and the distill backfill never checks the pause file.
  - The help text at [pause.go:81](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:81) says "Pause all background brain work on this machine". In these cases the user is told it is paused while hours of token spend carry on.
  - **Minimum fix:** return or print the resolution error, plus a line such as "no repository here; backfills in other repositories keep running".
  
  ### 3. HIGH: killing the backfill leaves its agent subprocesses running and spending tokens
  - [setup_spawn.go:81](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_spawn.go:81) kills only the pid.
  - The backfill runs `exec.CommandContext` agents (codex/claude, up to `--jobs N`) at [distill_cmd.go:2237](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:2237). The comment there says those agents spawn children of their own.

  - The process is started with `Setsid`, so killing the whole group would be possible. Given finding 1, though, killing a whole group that might belong to a stranger is worse.
  
  **Shared fix for findings 1–3:** when distill is launched as the setup backfill (an env var or flag set in `setupBackfillPlanFor`), have it check `backgroundPaused` between sessions or chunks and exit cleanly. Then `stop` doesn't kill anything. That fixes the stranger-kill, makes the pause cover every repo, and leaves no orphaned agents.

  - The worker writes `{"paused":true}` at [memory_cmd.go:1649-1651](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/memory_cmd.go:1649).   - `status`, `brief` freshness and `doctor` never call `backgroundPaused`.
  - So a `stop` the user has forgotten about shows up only as a brain that is going stale, with no reason given. Agents reading `brief` get stale context and no warning.
  - **Fix:** log a `paused` worker event, and show the pause in `status` and as a `brief` freshness axis.
  
  ### 5. MEDIUM: `backgroundPaused` throws its errors away
  - At [pause.go:29-36](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:29), a path-resolution failure and any `os.Stat` error other than ENOENT (EACCES, ENOTDIR, EIO) are all treated as "not paused", and nothing is recorded.
  - Failing open is fine. But the daemon, launched with `daemonEnv` (no XDG_* forwarding), can read a different state dir from the one `stop` wrote to, and neither side would show it.
  - **Fix:** return `(bool, error)`. Have the watch loop print `[watch] cannot read pause marker: …; continuing` and the worker log the same. Have `stop` print the path it wrote.
  
  ### 6. MEDIUM: `stop` doesn't say that work already in progress keeps going

  - A worker that got past the pause check still sleeps for up to `memoryWorkerMaxLeaseSleep` (1 minute) and then runs a full pass. The check at memory_cmd.go:1649 comes before that leased sleep and the prepass.
  - **Fix:** re-check after the leased sleep, and say "in-flight passes will finish" in the `stop` output.
  
  ### 7. MEDIUM: a broken backfill marker reads as "nothing to stop"
  - [setup_status.go:121-132](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/setup_status.go:121) treats a read error (permissions) or bad JSON the same as no marker.
  - That helper already existed, but it now drives a decision in `stop`.
  
  ### 8. LOW: benign exit race makes `stop` fail
  - If the backfill exits between the check and the kill, `proc.Kill` returns `os.ErrProcessDone`. `stop` has already printed "paused" and then exits non-zero ([pause.go:94-96](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:94)).
  - **Fix:** treat `errors.Is(err, os.ErrProcessDone)` as "not running".
  
  ### 9. LOW: the resume command is spelled three different ways
  - [pause.go:92](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:92) says `entire brain start`.
  - [workspace.go:425](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/workspace.go:425) hard-codes `entire-brain start`.
  - setup.go:928 uses `setupBrainCommand(brainCmd)`.
  
  ### 10. LOW: `start` and the help text overstate what resumes
  - `start` ([pause.go:111-115](vscode://file/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes/internal/cli/pause.go:111)) doesn't relaunch a backfill that `stop` killed, and doesn't mention it.
  - `backfill.json` still names the dead pid, and nothing records that the user stopped it.
  - The help text says paused work "runs after `start`". For the backfill, that depends on the capped `watch --distill` eventually clearing the backlog, which I haven't confirmed, or on running `setup` again.
  
  ### Handled well
  - `setBackgroundPaused` passes its errors up, and `start` correctly ignores ENOENT.
  - The paused watcher stays alive and logs why it is idle; the test checks that log.
  - Setup's skipped-backfill message says why and how to resume.
  - The `(0, nil)` return for a stale record whose lock is free is correct and tested.

     - MCP server startup (`nudgeMemoryAtStartup`), or

What changed after the reviews:
- **`stop` no longer kills anything.** Three reviewers independently showed the backfill kill could SIGKILL an unrelated process: the backfill's PID record is never cleared, and the "is it running" check accepts any distill lock, including the watcher's own. A running backfill is capped at 25 sessions by default, so letting it finish is bounded, and `stop` now says so.
- **The session-end hook honours the pause.** It runs a distill itself on every session end, so before this fix `stop` didn't stop the main per-session token spend.
- **The watcher re-checks before each workspace, and the worker re-checks after its leased sleep.** A `stop` that lands mid-pass now still takes effect.
- **`brain status` warns while paused**, so a forgotten `stop` doesn't look like a brain that quietly went stale.
- **Help text, messages and `docs/reference.md` match the code.** For example, `setup` now says "start, then re-run setup" instead of implying the backfill comes back on its own.

Declined: making `backgroundPaused` return errors. Treating an unreadable marker as "not paused" is deliberate, and `status` now covers the visibility concern.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/alex/.claude/skills/trail

# Trail

Capture the *Entire context* of a piece of work as a **trail** — the intent ("why/what"), with the branch's checkpoints/sessions as the evidence ("how/when"). Intentionally trail-only work creates one at spec-time; PR-bound work opens a human PR first and confirms automatic trail linking.

## The one rule that governs everything

A trail is keyed to a **single branch**. Checkpoints carry no trail link — the backend associates them **dynamically, by branch name**, at read time. Verified rule:

> A checkpoint appears under the trail **iff its commit is on the trail's branch and *ahead of the base*** — commits also on the base are excluded. "On the base" means recorded server-side, i.e. **pushed to `origin/<base>`**.

What follows:
- **Pre-spec discovery checkpoints attach automatically** — the trail need not have existed when they were made — *as long as their commits are on the trail's branch and not on the pushed base*.
- **Trail-only work may create at spec-time.** For PR-bound work, create the human-authored PR first and confirm automatic trail creation/linking before review; do not create a trail first.
- **Subsequent work attaches by itself.** Keep working on the branch and `git push` normally.

## When to use

A discovery cycle landed on a spec/design doc and implementation is about to start → identify whether work is intentionally trail-only or PR-bound. Create a trail at spec-time only for the trail-only path. Or the user runs `/trail` or asks to create / view / update a trail.

**When NOT to use:** trivial throwaway work. Repos whose `origin` isn't a supported forge error clearly (note: `entire://…/gh/owner/repo` remotes push through to GitHub and ARE supported; don't pre-check the URL).

## Workflow — intentionally trail-only work

1. **Find + read the spec** the discovery converged on (e.g. `docs/superpowers/specs/*-design.md`, or whatever was just written/referenced). Ask if unclear.
2. **Check for an existing trail** on the branch: `entire trail show`. If one exists → don't duplicate; go to **Updating** below.
3. **Resolve the branch:**
   - **On a feature branch** (≠ default) → just use it; `create` defaults `--branch` to the checked-out branch.
   - **On the default branch** (`main`/`master`) → cut a feature branch. Pass `--branch <slug> --checkout` (explicit name + switch to it). First check where discovery commits are (`git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD`, `git status -s`):
     - **Already pushed to `origin/<default>`** → *stranded*: those checkpoints are on the base and can't be retro-attached. Warn, then proceed.
     - **Uncommitted / committed only on local `<default>`** → *rescuable*: `git switch -c <slug>` (carries the commits + working changes), then `git branch -f <default> origin/<default>` (only with explicit user OK — rewrites local default). Verify `git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD` lists them.
4. **Draft title + description, confirm.** Title = concise intent. Put the why+what in `--body` (markdown), ending with a `Spec: <path>` line.
5. **Ask the status** (default is `open`): `draft` (intent defined, not active) or `open` (active / under review).
6. **Create only for intentionally trail-only work:**
   ```bash
   entire trail create --status open \
     --title "Token-bucket rate limiter for the public API" \
     --body "Throttle public-API requests per client with a refillable token bucket.

   Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-17-rate-limiter-design.md"
   ```
   Pass real newlines in `--body`, not literal `\n`.
7. **For PR-bound work:** do not run `entire trail create`. After implementation, open the human-authored PR first, then confirm its automatically created or linked trail before review. If linking is absent, report the integration problem rather than reverting to trail-first creation.

## PR-bound work — human PR first

For work that will use PR review or Bugbot, open the human-authored PR first. Confirm the automatically created or linked trail before starting review; Bugbot then sees the human-authored PR. Do not rely on automatic shadow-PR creation and do not run `entire trail create` for this path.

If automatic trail linking is missing, report the integration problem. Do not revert to trail-first ordering, create a replacement trail manually, or create a bot-authored shadow PR.

## Description / body

`--body` is a real, writable field again (a 2026-06 refactor wired it):
- **`create --body …`** → seeds the trail's description (editor document). ✅
- **`update --body …`** → updates it (no longer 400s). ✅
- **`entire trail show` DOES display the body** under a `Description:` section (corrected 2026-08-21; an earlier note here claimed otherwise). Markdown headings are flattened to plain lines, but the full text is rendered. An unset body shows `-- no description provided --`.

## Viewing / updating a trail

- **View:** `entire trail show [<num|id|branch>]` (defaults to the current branch's trail). Shows number, branch, base, status, author, phase, timestamps, and the body under `Description:`.
- **Update:** `entire trail update [--branch …] --status … --title … --body … --add-label … --remove-label …`. "Ready for review" = `--status open`; PR merge auto-sets `merged` (a merged trail rejects status changes). Trail status ≠ GitHub PR draft state — `gh pr ready` flips the PR.
- **Delete:** `entire trail delete [<number>]` (or `--branch` / current branch), confirm unless `--force`. Use to clean up a mistaken trail.

## Quick reference

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| Show a trail (current branch, or by num/id/branch) | `entire trail show [<trail>]` |
| Create | `entire trail create --title … --body … --status … [--branch … --checkout]` |
| Update | `entire trail update [--branch …] --status … --title … --body … --add-label …` |
| Delete | `entire trail delete [<number>] [--force]` |
| List (filter/JSON) | `entire trail list --status open\|any --author me --json -n 20` |
| Live finding/event stream | `entire trail watch [<number>]` |

**Status lifecycle:** `draft → open → merged → closed`. PR merge auto-transitions to `merged`; opening a PR doesn't change status; PR-auto-created trails default to `open`. Bare `entire trail` prints help. Run any subcommand with `--help` for exact flags.

## Common mistakes

- **Inventing commands/flags.** `entire trail report|ship|clean`, `--spec`, `--intent-file`, `--tags` appear in design RFDs but are **not** shipped. Use only the Quick reference commands.
- **Assuming `entire trail show` can't print the description** — it can, under `Description:`.
- **Cutting a fresh branch when discovery is already on `origin/<default>`** → those checkpoints strand (warn + proceed); if only local/unpushed, rescue them (workflow step 3).
- **Creating a second trail when one exists** → `create` finds-or-creates by branch and a duplicate errors; check `entire trail show` first and `update` instead.
- **Confusing trail status with the GitHub PR draft flag** → `gh pr ready` flips the PR, not `trail update`.
- **Assuming checkpoints synced** → a normal `git push` syncs them.
- **Creating a trail before a PR-bound Bugbot review** → use the human-authored PR first, then confirm automatic trail linking. If it is absent, report the integration problem; never revert to manual trail-first creation.

gh pr create --repo entireio/entire-brain --base main --head alex/control-background-processes --title 'feat(cli): add `brain stop`/`start` to pause background work machine-wide' --body-file - <<'EOF'
## Why

Background brain work had no off switch short of `setup --uninstall-daemon`, and that only removed the watcher. Three independent launchers keep work running:

- the launchd/systemd watcher (`KeepAlive`, so killing it just restarts it)
- event-driven `memory worker --once` launches from agent hooks, MCP startup and watch ticks, plus the worker's own delayed relaunch chain
- the session-end hook, which distills each ended session in-process
- `setup`'s detached fact backfill

## What

`entire brain stop` writes a `paused` marker in the plugin state dir (beside `watch-plan.json`); `entire brain start` removes it. Each launcher checks the marker itself rather than anything being killed:

| Path | While paused |
|---|---|
| Supervised watcher | stays loaded, skips work; re-checked per workspace so a mid-pass `stop` spares the rest |
| Memory worker | exits before the coordinator lease and again after the leased sleep; schedules no relaunch |
| Session-end hook | returns before export, hint, entity refresh and distill |
| `setup` backfill | skipped, with "start, then re-run setup" |
| `brain status` | adds a warning so a forgotten `stop` isn't a silently stale brain |

Nothing is lost: captured sessions stay canonical; reconciliation and the gated/manual distill pick them up after `start`.

**Deliberately not done:** `stop` does not kill an in-flight backfill. Review showed the existing `backfillRunning` check accepts any held distill lock and the pid record is never cleared, so a reused pid could be SIGKILLed. A running backfill is capped by `--backfill-budget` (25 by default) and finishes; `stop` says so.

The marker fails open (unreadable state dir ⇒ not paused) so a brain never silently stops updating on an I/O error.

## Testing

- `internal/cli/pause_test.go`: 11 behaviour tests, one per gate plus mid-pass and leased-sleep transitions, status warning, and start/stop round-trip
- `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l -s .` clean
- Smoke-tested the built binary's `stop`/`start` against isolated plugin dirs

EOF

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

#!/bin/bash
# Emits one line per actionable transition on PR #334 / Trail #250.
REPO=entireio/entire-brain
PR=334
WT=/Users/alex/.herdr/worktrees/entire-brain/alex-control-background-processes
prev=""
fails=0
while true; do
  pr=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json headRefOid,mergeable,state 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -z "$pr" ]; then
    fails=$((fails + 1))
    if [ "$fails" -eq 5 ]; then echo "DEGRADED: 5 consecutive PR fetch failures"; fi
    sleep 60
    continue
  fi
  fails=0
  head=$(echo "$pr" | jq -r .headRefOid)
  state=$(echo "$pr" | jq -r .state)
  mergeable=$(echo "$pr" | jq -r .mergeable)
  checks=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/commits/$head/check-runs?per_page=100" 2>/dev/null)
  bugbot=$(echo "$checks" | jq -r '[.check_runs[] | select(.name=="Cursor Bugbot")][0] | if . == null then "absent" else (.conclusion // "running") end')
  failed=$(echo "$checks" | jq -r '[.check_runs[] | select(.name!="Partial Gates" and .name!="Entire Gates" and (.conclusion=="failure" or .conclusion=="timed_out" or .conclusion=="cancelled")) | .name] | sort | join(",")')
  pending=$(echo "$checks" | jq -r '[.check_runs[] | select(.name!="Partial Gates" and .status!="completed")] | length')
  threads=$(gh api graphql -f query='query($o:String!,$r:String!,$n:Int!){repository(owner:$o,name:$r){pullRequest(number:$n){reviewThreads(first:100){nodes{isResolved}}}}}' -F o=entireio -F r=entire-brain -F n="$PR" --jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[] | select(.isResolved|not)] | length' 2>/dev/null)
  findings=$(entire trail finding list --freshness any --json 2>/dev/null </dev/null | jq -r '.counts.Open' 2>/dev/null)
  [ -z "$findings" ] && findings="?"
  cur="state=$state head=${head:0:8} mergeable=$mergeable bugbot=$bugbot failed=[$failed] pending=$pending threads=$threads findings=$findings"
  if [ "$cur" != "$prev" ]; then
    # Only emit when something actionable or terminal changed, not mid-run churn.
    key_cur=$(echo "$cur" | sed 's/ pending=[0-9]*//')
    key_prev=$(echo "$prev" | sed 's/ pending=[0-9]*//')
    if [ "$key_cur" != "$key_prev" ] || { [ "$pending" = "0" ] && [ -n "$prev" ]; }; then
      echo "PR#$PR $cur"
    fi
    prev="$cur"
  fi
  if [ "$state" = "MERGED" ] || [ "$state" = "CLOSED" ]; then
    echo "PR#$PR terminal: $state"
    exit 0
  fi
  sleep 60
done
